topic: Five-step needs analysis order
prompt: Which sequence correctly orders the five steps of the AV needs analysis process described in Chapter 3?
choices: Ask Questions → Review Existing Documentation → Evaluate the Site Environment / Benchmarking → Conduct Program Meetings → Create the Concept Design / Program Report
Create the Program Report → Order Equipment → Pull Cabling → Conduct Program Meetings → Ask Questions
Review Existing Documentation → Produce Shop Drawings → Install Racks → Verify ISCR Contrast → Ask Questions
Benchmarking → Final Acceptance → Systems Integration → Ask Questions → Create the Program Report
explanation: Needs analysis follows five steps before any equipment is chosen: Ask Questions, Review Existing Documentation, Evaluate the Site/Benchmarking, Conduct Program Meetings, and Create the Concept Design/Program Report.
studyNote: Memorize the 5-step needs analysis funnel: Questions → Docs → Site/Benchmark → Program Meetings → Program Report.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 3, pp. 41-48
rationales: Correct: Needs analysis moves from stakeholder questioning and document review through site/benchmark evaluation and program meetings to the written Concept Design / Program Report.
Not this one: Equipment ordering and cable pulling occur in the Construction phase long after the needs analysis and design phases.
Not this one: Shop drawings, rack installation, and ISCR contrast testing belong to implementation and verification, not initial discovery.
Not this one: Final acceptance and systems integration are closeout/deployment milestones, not needs-analysis steps.

topic: Exploration vs Sensation vs Instruction AV experiences
prompt: A museum commissions an interactive holographic gallery where visitors walk up to exhibits and manipulate virtual 3D artifacts to discover historical stories at their own pace. Which AV experience category best describes this environment?
choices: Instruction
Exploration
Sensation
Passive paging
explanation: Exploration describes an experience where participants actively discover and interact with real or virtual content, whereas Instruction transfers knowledge to absorbing learners and Sensation delights or amazes passive audiences.
studyNote: Match participant mode: Interact + Inform = Collaboration; Absorb + Inform = Instruction; Interact + Entertain = Exploration; Absorb + Entertain = Sensation.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 3, pp. 33-36
rationales: Not this one: Instruction transfers structured knowledge to participants who primarily absorb content rather than self-directing interactive discovery.
Correct: Exploration engages participants in discovering and interacting with real or virtual content in an entertaining, self-guided manner.
Not this one: Sensation aims to delight, amaze, or amuse participants who absorb the spectacle without interactive manipulation.
Not this one: Passive paging is not one of the four AV experience types on the Chapter 3 continuum.

topic: Comfortable horizontal and vertical head rotation limits
prompt: When evaluating audience seating angles during a sightline and ergonomics assessment, what is the comfortable horizontal head rotation range to either side of center, and why shouldn't the designer rely on neck rotation to widen the sustained viewing field?
choices: Comfortable horizontal head rotation is about 85 degrees each side, allowing seats to face away from the screen
Comfortable horizontal head rotation is about 10 degrees each side, and eyes cannot rotate at all
Comfortable horizontal head rotation is about 45 degrees each side (55 degrees average), and sustained neck rotation causes viewer fatigue over long sessions
Head rotation is unlimited on flat floors as long as swiveling chairs are used
explanation: While average horizontal head rotation reaches ~55° (and ~45° comfortably), forcing viewers to hold a rotated neck posture causes fatigue and strain over a session, so primary content must stay within the natural visual field.
studyNote: Horizontal head rotation: 45° comfortable (55° average); vertical head rotation: ≤30° comfortable. Do not count on neck movement to fix bad sightlines.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 4, pp. 74-77
rationales: Not this one: 85° far exceeds both comfortable (45°) and average (55°) horizontal head rotation limits.
Not this one: 10–20° is the stationary eye's word-recognition zone, whereas comfortable horizontal head rotation is about 45°.
Correct: Comfortable horizontal head rotation is ~45° (55° average), and relying on sustained neck twist or tilt fatigues the audience.
Not this one: Swiveling chairs introduce fidgeting and noise issues in camera rooms and do not change human cervical ergonomics.

topic: Passive viewing vs Full-motion video categories
prompt: An airport concourse display shows general flight-status tickers to passing travelers, while a dedicated screening room plays cinema films. Under ANSI/AVIXA V201.01 (ISCR), what minimum contrast ratios correspond to these two viewing categories?
choices: 15:1 for the concourse display and 50:1 for the cinema screening room
50:1 for the concourse display and 7:1 for the cinema screening room
80:1 for both environments
7:1 for Passive Viewing (concourse display) and 80:1 for Full-Motion Video (cinema screening room)
explanation: General transit signage where viewers glance briefly without making critical decisions is Passive Viewing (7:1 minimum contrast), whereas cinema/home-theater playback is Full-Motion Video (80:1 minimum contrast).
studyNote: ISCR minimums: Passive = 7:1, BDM = 15:1, ADM = 50:1, Full-motion video = 80:1.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 5, pp. 91-94, 102-105
rationales: Not this one: 15:1 is for Basic Decision-Making (BDM) and 50:1 is for Analytical Decision-Making (ADM).
Not this one: This reverses the detail and contrast hierarchy between casual glance signage and cinema video.
Not this one: Requiring 80:1 in a sunlit airport concourse is neither required for passive viewing nor practical.
Correct: Passive viewing requires at least 7:1 contrast, while full-motion video requires at least 80:1 contrast.

topic: Discoverability vs Understanding in user interface design
prompt: In Chapter 15's human-centered control design framework, how do the two fundamental goals of 'discoverability' and 'understanding' differ when an end user walks up to a room control panel?
choices: Discoverability means the user can figure out what actions are possible and where/how to perform them; understanding means the user can tell how the system is meant to be used and what the controls mean
Discoverability measures the RF signal strength of a Wi-Fi touch panel, while understanding measures CPU clock speed
Discoverability applies only to blind users, while understanding applies only to programmers
Both terms refer to the number of RS-232 ports on the back of the control processor
explanation: Human-centered design rests on discoverability (knowing what actions are possible and how to trigger them) and understanding (grasping how the product is meant to be used).
studyNote: Discoverability = 'What can I do and where do I press?' Understanding = 'How is this system meant to be used?'
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 304-307
rationales: Correct: Discoverability lets users see possible actions and how to perform them; understanding lets them grasp how the system works.
Not this one: RF signal strength and CPU clock speed are hardware specs, not human-centered UI concepts.
Not this one: Discoverability and understanding apply to every user interacting with any control interface.
Not this one: Serial port count is a hardware capacity metric, not a user-interface characteristic.

task: Review or formulate client technology master plan
topic: Routine network bandwidth ceiling (50% of ready capacity)
prompt: When reviewing a client's shared enterprise LAN capacity for an AV technology master plan, what maximum percentage of 'ready (available) capacity' does Chapter 16 recommend budgeting for routine AV network traffic?
choices: 95% of rated link capacity
No more than 50% of ready (available) capacity on a shared network (though a dedicated, isolated AV LAN can utilize a higher share)
100% of nominal switch port speed
2% of available capacity
explanation: On a shared network, routine AV traffic should be planned to consume no more than 50% of ready (available) capacity so bursts do not saturate the LAN; an isolated AV-only LAN can safely use a higher percentage.
studyNote: Shared network routine AV cap = ≤50% of ready capacity (and streaming share ≈ 20% of rated capacity: 70% × 30%).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 321-323
rationales: Not this one: Planning for 95% of rated capacity guarantees severe packet loss and congestion during normal traffic peaks.
Correct: Chapter 16 caps routine AV use at no more than 50% of ready capacity on shared networks, while noting an isolated AV LAN may use more.
Not this one: Rated capacity is never 100% usable in real packet networks due to protocol overhead and burst contention.
Not this one: 2% is unnecessarily restrictive; 50% of ready capacity (or ~20% of rated for streaming) is the book's benchmark.

task: Review or formulate client technology master plan
topic: IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi generations and 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow) role
prompt: While reviewing wireless standards for a client's campus master plan, how should the designer distinguish IEEE 802.11n/ac/ax (Wi-Fi 4/5/6) from IEEE 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow)?
choices: 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow) is designed for uncompressed 8K video over IP
802.11n is Wi-Fi 6E and operates exclusively at 60 GHz

802.11n (Wi-Fi 4), 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5), and 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6/6E) are high-throughput WLAN standards, whereas sub-1 GHz 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow) is suited for low-data-rate, long-range AV control and IoT rather than AV-over-IP media
All IEEE 802.11 standards use wired coaxial BNC connectors
explanation: Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n), Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac), and Wi-Fi 6/6E (802.11ax) serve general wireless LAN traffic, whereas 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow) trades throughput for low power and range—making it suitable for AV control, not AV-over-IP streaming.
studyNote: 802.11n = Wi-Fi 4; 802.11ac = Wi-Fi 5; 802.11ax = Wi-Fi 6/6E; 802.11ah (HaLow) = AV control/IoT only, not AVoIP.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 326-328
rationales: Not this one: 802.11ah has low data rates intended for sensors and control, not high-bitrate video.
Not this one: 802.11n is Wi-Fi 4 (2.4/5 GHz), while Wi-Fi 6/6E is 802.11ax.
Correct: 802.11n/ac/ax map to Wi-Fi 4/5/6, while 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow) is suited for AV control rather than AV-over-IP media streams.
Not this one: IEEE 802.11 defines wireless LAN (Wi-Fi), whereas IEEE 802.3 defines Ethernet.

task: Review or formulate client technology master plan
topic: Security posture classification (lax, realistic, paranoid)
prompt: When formulating the security section of a client's technology master plan, who sets the organization's security posture (often described colloquially as lax, realistic, or paranoid), and what are the seven steps to determine it?
choices: The AV equipment manufacturer sets the posture after installation
The electrical subcontractor chooses the posture based on conduit size
The acoustical consultant sets the posture using STC ratings

The client sets the security posture; the designer determines it by learning the client's mission, concept of operations, data importance, risk profile, stakeholders, governance structure, and project constraints
explanation: Security posture is always set by the client, not the AV designer; the designer uncovers it through seven steps: mission, concept of operations, data importance, risk profile, stakeholders, governance, and project constraints.
studyNote: The client sets the security posture; the designer surfaces it early before design sign-off using the 7-step posture discovery process.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 18, pp. 370-374
rationales: Not this one: Manufacturers build security features, but only the client organization owns its risk tolerance and security posture.
Not this one: Electrical subcontractors install raceways and power, not enterprise information-security policy.
Not this one: STC measures airborne speech isolation, though physical acoustic privacy is one input to meeting confidentiality.
Correct: The client defines the security posture, and the CTS-D documents it by evaluating mission, operations, data value, risk profile, stakeholders, governance, and constraints.

task: Review or formulate client technology master plan
topic: Direct-view display luminance range (350 cd/m2 indoor vs 6500 cd/m2 outdoor)
prompt: A retail client's technology master plan covers both indoor conference rooms and sun-facing outdoor storefront digital signage. What typical direct-view display luminance range distinguishes indoor meeting displays from outdoor signage displays?
choices: About 350 cd/m² (nits) for indoor hospitality and meeting rooms, scaling up to about 6,500 cd/m² for outdoor high-ambient signage
About 5 cd/m² for indoor meeting rooms and 50 cd/m² for outdoor signage
Exactly 10,000 cd/m² for dark indoor boardrooms and 100 cd/m² for outdoor stadiums
Luminance is measured in ohms and is identical indoors and outdoors
explanation: Direct-view flat panels typically operate around 350 cd/m² (nits) in indoor meeting or hospitality environments and up to roughly 6,500 cd/m² to overcome direct sunlight in outdoor digital signage.
studyNote: Direct-view display brightness benchmark: ~350 cd/m² (nits) indoor meeting room vs. up to ~6,500 cd/m² outdoor signage.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 5, pp. 114-116
rationales: Correct: Indoor commercial displays typically start around 350 cd/m², whereas outdoor sunlight-readable signage reaches up to ~6,500 cd/m².
Not this one: 5 to 50 cd/m² is far too dim for daylight or normal room viewing.
Not this one: 10,000 cd/m² indoors would cause severe disability glare, while 100 cd/m² outdoors would be invisible in sunlight.
Not this one: Luminance is measured in candelas per square meter (cd/m² or nits) or foot-lamberts (fL), not ohms.

task: Review or formulate client technology master plan
topic: Computer-driven vs built-in vs traditional processor control trade-offs
prompt: When evaluating control platforms for a client's technology master plan, what is the primary vulnerability of relying on a 'computer-driven' control system running on a standard commercial desktop operating system?
choices: It cannot display colors on a monitor
It is dependent on commercial operating-system updates and OS version lifecycles, and may not scale reliably across large enterprise deployments
It can communicate only via mechanical pneumatic tubes
It requires no electricity to operate
explanation: While computer-driven control supports BYOD and web access at low hardware cost, it depends on third-party operating system versions/updates and often struggles to scale with the reliability of dedicated control processors.
studyNote: Control platform risks: Traditional = cost/proprietary training; Computer-driven = OS dependency/scaling; Cloud = outage cost; Custom = owner maintenance burden.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 299-302
rationales: Not this one: Standard computers drive graphical monitors easily; the risk lies in OS lifecycle stability and scalability.
Correct: Computer-driven control systems depend on OS versions and automated patches that can break drivers and limit enterprise scalability.
Not this one: Computer-driven systems use standard USB, Ethernet, and wireless interfaces.
Not this one: All electronic control platforms require electrical power.

task: Generate and/or Review the Program Report
topic: Alternative industry names for the Concept Design / Program Report
prompt: When reviewing project documentation across different architectural and consulting firms, which alternative titles refer to the same deliverable as the 'Concept Design / Program Report'?
choices: The As-Built Redline Set, the Punch List, or the Bill of Lading
The Request for Quotation (RFQ), the Change Order, or the Lien Waiver
The AV Narrative, the Discovery Phase Report, or the Return Brief
The Cable Pull Schedule, the Rack Elevation, or the DiffServ Table
explanation: Chapter 3 notes that the Concept Design / Program Report—which records nontechnical functional descriptions and probable cost after needs analysis—is also called the AV narrative, discovery phase report, or return brief.
studyNote: Concept Design / Program Report synonyms: AV Narrative, Discovery Phase Report, Return Brief.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 3, pp. 46-49
rationales: Not this one: As-builts and punch lists are closeout documents, and a bill of lading is a freight shipping document.
Not this one: RFQs, change orders, and lien waivers are commercial procurement/contract administration documents.
Correct: The Concept Design / Program Report is commonly referred to as the AV narrative, discovery phase report, or return brief.
Not this one: Cable schedules, rack elevations, and DiffServ tables are detailed technical engineering documents produced later.

task: Generate and/or Review the Program Report
topic: Closed-ended stakeholder questions for factual project constraints
prompt: While gathering inputs for the Program Report, the designer asks the client's construction manager, 'On what exact date will the room be available for AV installation?' Which interview question type is this, and when is it used?
choices: Open-ended question, used to explore broad philosophical goals
Directive question, used to persuade the client to buy a specific projector
Rhetorical question, used to avoid recording an answer
Closed-ended question, used to obtain specific, unambiguous facts such as dates, counts, or yes/no confirmations
explanation: Closed-ended questions ask for a specific fact, number, date, or yes/no response, complementing open-ended questions (which explore needs broadly) and directive questions (which guide toward a solution).
studyNote: Question types: Open-ended = get client talking/thinking; Closed-ended = get specific facts/dates; Directive = guide toward a practical option.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 3, pp. 42-44
rationales: Not this one: Open-ended questions invite expansive narrative answers rather than a single calendar date.
Not this one: Directive questions steer a stakeholder toward a design choice rather than requesting a schedule date.
Not this one: Every question in a needs analysis should gather actionable stakeholder information.
Correct: Asking for a specific construction start date is a closed-ended question designed to capture a concrete fact.

task: Generate and/or Review the Program Report
topic: Furniture dimension standards for adult conference tables and chairs
prompt: When reviewing space-planning layouts in a Program Report for an adult conference room, what are the standard typical table height, optimal table width per seated person, and aisle circulation clearance?
choices: Typical table height is 735 mm (29 in.), optimal table width per seated person is 600 to 750 mm (24 to 30 in.) with 450 to 600 mm depth, and passageway/aisle circulation is 750 to 900 mm (30 to 36 in.)
Typical table height is 1,200 mm (47 in.), table width per person is 200 mm (8 in.), and aisle clearance is 250 mm (10 in.)
Typical table height is 400 mm (16 in.) and each seated person requires 3,000 mm of table edge
Counter height is 450 mm (18 in.) and movable chairs are 1,200 mm wide
explanation: Standard adult furniture ergonomics specify a 735 mm (29 in.) table height (range 635–815 mm), 915 mm (36 in.) counter height, 600–750 mm (24–30 in.) table width per person, 750–900 mm (30–36 in.) aisle circulation, and ≥1,220 mm (48 in.) from seated table edge to obstruction.
studyNote: Table height = 735 mm (29 in.); per-person width = 600–750 mm (24–30 in.); aisle = 750–900 mm (30–36 in.); table-to-wall = ≥1,220 mm (48 in.).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 4, pp. 82-86
rationales: Correct: These match Chapter 4's ergonomic reference tables for adult table height, per-person workspace, and aisle circulation.
Not this one: 1,200 mm is above standing counter height and 200 mm per person is impossibly narrow.
Not this one: 400 mm is coffee-table height, not a standard work or conference table.
Not this one: Standard counter height is 915 mm (36 in.) and movable chair width is 560–660 mm (22–26 in.).

task: Generate and/or Review the Program Report
topic: Estimate vs Quote vs Opinion of Probable Cost in program documentation
prompt: After the client approves the Concept Design / Program Report and its initial Opinion of Probable Cost, the designer develops an approximate line-item calculation of equipment and labor costs during design development. What is this intermediate cost figure called?
choices: A Binding Vendor Quote
An Estimate
A Final Closeout Invoice
A Liquidated Damages Penalty
explanation: On the budget terminology ladder, an Opinion of Probable Cost is an early pre-design projection, an Estimate is an approximate line-item calculation of equipment and labor, and a Quote is a detailed, enforceable price offer based on the completed design.
studyNote: Cost progression: Opinion of Probable Cost (early guess) → Estimate (line-item approximation) → Quote (enforceable offer after design).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 3, pp. 48-51
rationales: Not this one: A Quote is an enforceable offer submitted by a provider in response to an RFP after the AV design is complete.
Correct: An Estimate is an approximate line-item calculation of equipment and labor that is more accurate than an early Opinion of Probable Cost.
Not this one: An invoice bills for work performed under an executed contract.
Not this one: Liquidated damages are contractual penalties for late completion, not a design cost projection.

task: Generate and/or Review the Program Report
topic: Sightline vs viewing angle distinction in program space planning
prompt: When documenting display and presenter geometry in a Program Report, why must the designer evaluate both 'sightline' and 'viewing angle' as two separate criteria?
choices: Sightline and viewing angle are identical synonyms for projector throw ratio
Sightline applies only to audio loudspeakers, while viewing angle applies only to microphones
A seat can have a completely unobstructed sightline to a lectern or screen while still suffering from an excessive off-axis viewing angle that distorts image geometry and lowers contrast
Viewing angle matters only when the audience is blindfolded
explanation: Sightline is an unobstructed line of view between the observer and the target, whereas viewing angle measures how far off-axis the observer sits relative to the display surface; good sightlines can coexist with poor viewing angles.
studyNote: Unobstructed sightline ≠ good viewing angle! Check both vertical/horizontal sightline clearances and the 60° DISCAS viewing arc.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 4, pp. 76-81
rationales: Not this one: Throw ratio is an optical lens parameter, whereas sightline and viewing angle describe viewer geometry.
Not this one: Both sightline and viewing angle are visual human-factors criteria.
Correct: A front-corner seat may have zero physical obstruction (clear sightline) yet sit too far off-axis (poor viewing angle) to read the screen.
Not this one: Both metrics govern visual perception for sighted occupants.

topic: Task illuminance target range (150 lux min, 320 lux preferred)
prompt: When coordinating work-surface lighting with the lighting designer for a presentation and training room where attendees take paper notes during slide presentations, what task illuminance levels does Chapter 8 recommend?
choices: 10 lux (1 fc) minimum and 25 lux (2.5 fc) preferred
1,500 lux (140 fc) minimum and 3,200 lux (300 fc) preferred
0 lux across the entire seating area
150 lux (14 fc) minimum and 320 lux (30 fc) preferred, kept off the projection screen
explanation: Chapter 8 specifies a minimum of 150 lux (14 fc) and a preferred level of 320 lux (30 fc) for horizontal task lighting on work surfaces, zoned and aimed away from projection screens.
studyNote: Task light levels: 150 lux (14 fc) minimum; 320 lux (30 fc) preferred; keep within ÷3 to ×3 of screen white luminance.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 8, pp. 172-176
rationales: Not this one: 10–25 lux is too dim for comfortable reading and note-taking.
Not this one: 1,500–3,200 lux is surgical/studio intensity that would wash out projection screens and cause glare.
Not this one: Total darkness prevents note-taking and safe movement.
Correct: 150 lux (14 fc) minimum and 320 lux (30 fc) preferred support reading and note-taking while preserving screen contrast when properly zoned.

topic: Lamp vs luminaire terminology and luminous efficacy (lm/W)
prompt: When writing lighting coordination specifications for the architectural team, what is the standard distinction between a 'lamp' and a 'luminaire,' and what does 'efficacy' measure?
choices: A lamp is the light-producing element (bulb, tube, or LED chip array), whereas a luminaire is the complete lighting instrument (lamp, optics, housing, mount, power supply, and control); efficacy measures energy efficiency in lumens per watt (initial lumens ÷ nominal power)
A luminaire is the replaceable glass bulb, and a lamp is the ceiling mounting clamp; efficacy measures color rendering from 0 to 100
Efficacy is the correlated color temperature measured in degrees Celsius
A lamp and a luminaire both refer exclusively to 19-inch equipment racks
explanation: 'Lamp' refers to the light source itself, while 'luminaire' is the complete lighting fixture assembly; luminous efficacy equals initial lumen output divided by nominal electrical watts (lm/W).
studyNote: Lamp = light source; Luminaire = complete fixture (optics, housing, PSU, mount); Efficacy = lumens ÷ watts (lm/W).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 8, pp. 166-171
rationales: Correct: Lamp is the light-emitting element, luminaire is the complete fixture, and efficacy is lumens per watt.
Not this one: This reverses lamp and luminaire, and color accuracy is measured by CRI/Rf rather than efficacy.
Not this one: Correlated color temperature is expressed in Kelvin (K, never degrees), not efficacy.
Not this one: Racks are structural enclosures covered in Chapter 9.

topic: Direct glare vs indirect glare (veiling reflections) in display spaces
prompt: During an interior coordination review for a boardroom with large windows and a polished marble table, how should the CTS-D distinguish 'direct glare' from 'indirect glare' (veiling reflections)?
choices: Direct glare occurs only at night, while indirect glare occurs only at noon

Direct glare is bright light from a luminaire or window entering the viewer's eyes or camera lens directly, whereas indirect glare (veiling reflection) is bright light reflected off a glossy surface (like a polished table or glass bezel) into the eyes or lens
Indirect glare increases the Image System Contrast Ratio (ISCR) to 100:1
Direct glare is an acoustic reflection arriving after 50 milliseconds
explanation: Direct glare comes straight from a light source into the eye or camera; indirect glare (veiling reflections) bounces off shiny tabletops, floors, or glass displays to veil the image and reduce contrast.
studyNote: Direct glare = light source straight into eye/camera; Indirect glare (veiling reflection) = specular bounce off shiny surfaces.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 8, pp. 165-167, 179
rationales: Not this one: Both direct and indirect glare can occur at any time from either artificial luminaires or daylight.
Correct: Direct glare enters the eye/lens directly from the source; indirect glare reflects off specular surfaces as veiling reflections.
Not this one: Veiling reflections raise the minimum black luminance and severely degrade contrast ratio.
Not this one: Delayed acoustic reflections are echoes, not optical glare.

topic: ADA reach ranges for side approach (15-54 in) vs forward approach (15-48 in)
prompt: When coordinating wall-mounted AV control panel heights with the architect and structural framing team under cited ADA accessibility rules, how do the permissible mounting height ranges differ between a side approach and a forward-only approach?
choices: Side approach allows 100 mm to 2,000 mm AFF, while forward approach allows only 1,500 mm AFF
Both side and forward approaches require controls to be mounted at 1,800 mm (71 in.) AFF

Side approach allows controls between 380 mm (15 in.) and 1,370 mm (54 in.) above the floor, whereas forward-only approach restricts controls to between 380 mm (15 in.) and 1,220 mm (48 in.) above the floor
Controls must be mounted on the ceiling above 2,030 mm (80 in.)
explanation: Per the ADA guidance cited in Chapter 9, operator controls must sit between 380 mm (15 in.) and 1,370 mm (54 in.) AFF for a side approach, and between 380 mm (15 in.) and 1,220 mm (48 in.) AFF for a forward-only approach.
studyNote: ADA control heights: Forward approach = 380–1,220 mm (15–48 in.); Side approach = 380–1,370 mm (15–54 in.); Wall protrusion = ≤100 mm (4 in.); Headroom = ≥2,030 mm (80 in.).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 185-188
rationales: Not this one: 2,000 mm and 1,500 mm exceed wheelchair reach limits.
Not this one: 1,800 mm (71 in.) is inaccessible to seated wheelchair users.
Correct: Side approach spans 380–1,370 mm (15–54 in.) AFF, and forward approach spans 380–1,220 mm (15–48 in.) AFF.
Not this one: 2,030 mm (80 in.) is the minimum overhead clearance under ceiling-hung hazards in a circulation path.

topic: Structural fastener failure modes: shear, tension, pull-out, and improper load math
prompt: When reviewing overhead and wall mounting designs with a structural engineer, what is the difference between 'shearing' failure, 'tensile' failure, and 'pull-out' failure of a mounting fastener?
choices: All three terms mean the paint on the bracket peeled off
Shearing is corrosion from humidity, tensile is electrical arcing, and pull-out is software crashing
Shearing is the bolt unscrewing due to vibration, while pull-out is the display glass cracking

Shearing occurs when weight acts perpendicular across the bolt shaft slicing it; tensile failure occurs when axial load stretches, twists, or snaps the fastener; pull-out occurs when the anchor or bolt tears out of the wall or ceiling substrate
explanation: Fasteners fail in distinct ways: shear slices across the bolt cross-section under perpendicular load, tensile stress stretches/breaks the bolt along its length, and pull-out extracts the anchor from the host material.
studyNote: Fastener failure modes: Shear (slicing across shaft), Tensile (stretching/snapping along axis), Pull-out (leaving wall/ceiling substrate).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 187-191
rationales: Not this one: These are mechanical structural failure modes, not cosmetic finish defects.
Not this one: Shear, tension, and pull-out are mechanical force failures on fasteners and substrates.
Not this one: Unscrewing is rotational loosening on unlocked threads, not shear or pull-out.
Correct: Shear acts across the bolt, tensile force stretches/breaks the bolt axially, and pull-out extracts the fastener from the wall or ceiling.

topic: ASTM/SAE bolt head radial markings vs ISO numeric property classes
prompt: During a pre-installation structural inspection, you examine two bolts proposed for a heavy overhead rigging bracket: one is an ASTM/SAE bolt with zero raised radial lines on its head, and the other has three raised radial lines. How should you evaluate them?
choices: Reject the unmarked bolt (ASTM/SAE Grade 2) and use at least the three-line bolt (ASTM/SAE Grade 5) or an ISO Property Class 8.8 (or higher) structural fastener
Use the unmarked bolt because fewer lines on an ASTM bolt head indicate higher strength
Reject both because only nylon bolts are permitted for overhead rigging
ISO Property Class 4.6 is stronger than ISO Property Class 10.9
explanation: On ASTM/SAE bolts, more radial bumps/lines on the head mean higher strength (no marks = Grade 2, three marks = Grade 5, six marks = Grade 8); on ISO metric bolts, higher numbers (such as 8.8 or 10.9) indicate higher strength. Overhead AV mounts require at least Grade 5 or ISO 8.8.
studyNote: Bolt ratings: Require ≥ ASTM/SAE Grade 5 (3 radial lines on head) or ≥ ISO Property Class 8.8. Never use unmarked Grade 2 hardware.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 189-192
rationales: Correct: Zero head markings indicate low-strength Grade 2 hardware; three radial lines indicate Grade 5, which (along with ISO 8.8+) is the minimum for structural AV mounts.
Not this one: More radial markings on an ASTM/SAE bolt head indicate higher tensile strength, not lower.
Not this one: Overhead mounts require rated high-strength steel fasteners.
Not this one: ISO numeric classes rise with strength, so 10.9 and 8.8 are much stronger than 4.6.

task: Coordinate with mechanical, electrical, and plumbing professionals
topic: Isolated ground vs standard protective earth vs technical power
prompt: When coordinating earthing/grounding systems with an electrical engineer for a broadcast studio or sensitive analog audio rack, how does an 'isolated ground' (or 'technical power') system reduce ground-loop hum while maintaining electrical safety?
choices: It completely disconnects all equipment chassis from earth ground so fault current has no return path

It provides an insulated equipment safety-ground conductor separated from local panel neutrals and building steel all the way back to the main service distribution board (star ground point), keeping noisy neutral return currents off the AV safety ground while preserving fault protection
It wires the green safety-ground conductor directly to the 208 V hot phase
It replaces copper branch circuits with unshielded plastic water pipes
explanation: Isolated ground (and technical power) keeps the protective-earth conductor continuous for safety fault protection, but insulates it from local subpanel enclosures and neutral returns until a single bond at the main service entrance.
studyNote: Isolated ground / technical power = continuous safety earth insulated from local subpanels/building steel back to the main service ground point.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 211-215
rationales: Not this one: Removing the earth path is illegal and creates a lethal shock hazard during a chassis fault.

Correct: An isolated ground maintains an unbroken low-impedance safety earth back to the main distribution board while preventing local neutral/structural currents from circulating on AV cable shields.
Not this one: Connecting the ground wire to a hot phase energizes every chassis to mains voltage.
Not this one: Plastic pipes are non-conductive and cannot serve as an equipment grounding conductor.

task: Coordinate with mechanical, electrical, and plumbing professionals
topic: Capacitive reactance (XC) vs inductive reactance (XL) in AC circuits
prompt: In AC electrical and audio circuits, how do capacitive reactance (XC) and inductive reactance (XL) behave as signal frequency increases, and how does long cable capacitance affect analog signals?
choices: Both XC and XL remain constant at all frequencies like pure DC resistance
XC rises with frequency and causes low-frequency bass loss in long cables

Capacitive reactance (XC) decreases as frequency rises (causing shunt cable capacitance to attenuate high frequencies on long unbalanced runs), whereas inductive reactance (XL) increases as frequency rises
Inductive reactance (XL) occurs only in optical fiber cables
explanation: Capacitive reactance XC falls as frequency rises (so parallel capacitance between conductors in a long cable increasingly shunts high frequencies to ground), while inductive reactance XL rises as frequency rises; combined with DC resistance R, they form total AC impedance Z.
studyNote: Frequency ↑ → Capacitive reactance XC ↓ (shunts high frequencies in long cables) and Inductive reactance XL ↑.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 206-209
rationales: Not this one: Pure resistance (R) is frequency-independent, whereas reactance (XC and XL) varies with frequency.
Not this one: XC falls as frequency rises; shunt capacitance across a cable rolls off high frequencies, not bass.
Correct: XC drops with rising frequency (causing high-frequency roll-off in capacitive cables) while XL rises with frequency.
Not this one: Optical fiber carries light pulses and has neither electrical inductance nor capacitance.

task: Coordinate with mechanical, electrical, and plumbing professionals
topic: Signal ground vs supply ground vs safety ground distinction
prompt: Why does Chapter 10 insist on distinguishing among 'signal ground,' 'supply ground,' and 'safety ground' when coordinating electrical and system drawings?
choices: All three terms refer to the hot phase conductor in a 240 V circuit
Only safety ground carries audio waveforms between mixers and amplifiers
Supply ground is used only on wireless Bluetooth connections

They represent three mutually exclusive functions—the reference point for internal electronics/signals, the current return path of a power supply, and the uninterrupted protective-earth fault path on conductive enclosures—and conflating them leads to wiring errors and ground loops
explanation: Signal ground, supply ground, and safety ground perform distinct roles; using the generic word 'ground' without naming which of the three is meant causes dangerous or noisy miswiring.
studyNote: Always name which 'ground' you mean: Signal ground (audio/video reference), Supply ground (power return), or Safety ground (protective earth / EGC).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 210-214
rationales: Not this one: None of the three ground categories is a live phase conductor.
Not this one: Safety ground (protective earth) must never be used as the normal signal or load return path.
Not this one: Supply ground is the DC/AC power return reference in electronic supplies.
Correct: Separating signal ground, supply ground, and safety ground prevents dangerous faults and ground-loop noise.

task: Coordinate with IT and network security professionals
topic: Physical topology vs logical topology independence in AV networks
prompt: When reviewing network diagrams with the IT department, what is the difference between a network's 'physical topology' and its 'logical topology'?
choices: Physical topology shows where hardware nodes and cables are physically located and wired, whereas logical topology describes how data actually flows between network segments and VLANs; the two are independent of each other
Physical topology applies only to Wi-Fi networks, while logical topology applies only to coaxial cables
Logical topology measures the weight of the Ethernet switches in kilograms
Physical and logical topologies must always be drawn as a single ring
explanation: Physical topology maps the physical placement of nodes and cabling links, whereas logical topology maps how data frames and packets flow across segments and VLANs; they are independent and both are needed for capacity planning.
studyNote: Physical topology = where cables/switches sit; Logical topology = how data flows across segments/VLANs.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 319-322
rationales: Correct: Physical topology describes physical device/cable layout while logical topology describes data flow paths.
Not this one: Both wired and wireless networks have physical and logical topologies.
Not this one: Rack weight is a structural metric, not a logical network topology.
Not this one: Modern Ethernet uses physical star/hierarchical topologies while supporting diverse logical flows.

task: Coordinate with IT and network security professionals
topic: Managed switch vs unmanaged switch requirements for AV over IP
prompt: Why must an AV designer specify 'managed switches' rather than 'unmanaged switches' when coordinating a network that carries Dante, AES67, AVB, or multicast AV-over-IP traffic?
choices: Unmanaged switches double the bit rate of Category 6A cables automatically

Unmanaged switches offer no configuration, whereas managed switches allow the administrator to configure VLAN isolation, DiffServ QoS priority queues, IGMP snooping/querier, port speeds, and traffic monitoring required by real-time AV
Managed switches work without IP addresses or MAC addresses
Unmanaged switches block all unicast HTTP traffic by default
explanation: Unmanaged switches simply forward frames with zero configuration; networked AV protocols require managed switches to configure QoS, VLANs, IGMP multicast control, and port diagnostics.
studyNote: Real-time networked AV requires managed switches for VLANs, QoS (DiffServ), IGMP snooping, and port monitoring.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 321-324, 338-341
rationales: Not this one: Cable category and transceiver standards—not unmanaged switches—set physical link speed.
Correct: Managed switches provide the VLAN, QoS, IGMP, and monitoring controls essential for real-time AV-over-IP.
Not this one: Every Layer 2/3 managed switch uses MAC and IP addressing.
Not this one: Unmanaged switches pass all Ethernet frames indiscriminately without security filtering.

task: Coordinate with IT and network security professionals
topic: Threat logic formula (Threat = Vulnerability + Actor/Exploit Intent)
prompt: In Chapter 18's networked AV security framework, how is a security 'threat' defined in relation to a 'vulnerability,' and what baseline assumption should the designer make about known vulnerabilities?
choices: A vulnerability is harmless unless the device is connected to a 70 V loudspeaker line
A threat exists only when a firewall is turned off during business hours

A threat equals a vulnerability plus someone or something that wants to exploit it; designers must assume that any known vulnerability will eventually be exploited and scale protection to the value of the asset guarded
Known vulnerabilities should be ignored if the AV system is located inside an office building
explanation: Chapter 18 defines threat logic as: Threat = Vulnerability + an actor/process seeking to exploit it, and advises designers to assume known vulnerabilities will be exploited.
studyNote: Threat = Vulnerability + someone/something that wants to exploit it. Assume known vulnerabilities WILL be exploited.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 18, pp. 376-379
rationales: Not this one: Cyber and physical vulnerabilities exist independent of loudspeaker distribution voltage.
Not this one: Threats can originate from internal users, invited malware, or physical access even behind a firewall.
Correct: A vulnerability combined with an exploiting actor creates a threat, and known vulnerabilities must be assumed exploitable.
Not this one: Insider threats and lateral network movement occur frequently inside office buildings.

topic: Five properties of sound in an acoustical review
prompt: When reviewing a space with an acoustical professional, which five sequential properties of sound frame the evaluation from source to listener?
choices: Sampling, Quantizing, Encoding, Packetizing, and Decoding
Key, Fill, Backlight, Wash, and Accent
Hue, Saturation, Luminance, Contrast, and Acuity
Production (source), Propagation (pathway), Control (generation/path management), Interaction (how materials respond), and Reception (how ears and brains respond)
explanation: Chapter 11 organizes acoustical analysis around five properties of sound: Production, Propagation, Control, Interaction, and Reception.
studyNote: Five properties of sound (Ch 11): Production → Propagation → Control → Interaction → Reception.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 225-227
rationales: Not this one: Those are digital signal conversion and streaming steps from Chapter 12.
Not this one: Those are the videoconference lighting functional groups from Chapter 8.
Not this one: Those are visual and color perception parameters from Chapters 5 and 8.
Correct: Acousticians evaluate Production, Propagation, Control, Interaction, and Reception.

topic: Conservation of acoustic energy at a boundary (reflection, absorption, transmission)
prompt: When sound energy strikes an interior partition wall, which three physical outcomes occur, and why can't electronic equalization 'fix' a highly reverberant or poorly isolated room?
choices: Energy is conserved across reflection, absorption, and transmission (whatever is not absorbed or transmitted is reflected); room acoustics are governed by physical geometry, mass, and surface treatment, so electronic EQ cannot stop reflections or transmission
All sound striking a wall is destroyed by destructive interference
Graphic equalization absorbs reverberant decay tails inside the air volume
High absorption coefficients on carpet block 100 Hz subwoofer transmission through walls
explanation: At any boundary, incident sound energy splits into reflected, absorbed, and transmitted fractions; because reverberation and standing waves are physical room behaviors, there is no way to 'equalize a room' electronically.
studyNote: Boundary energy conservation: Incident = Reflected + Absorbed + Transmitted. You cannot equalize a room's physical acoustics!
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11 & Chapter 14, pp. 226-228, 291-293
rationales: Correct: Sound at a boundary is reflected, absorbed, or transmitted, and physical acoustic defects must be solved acoustically rather than with EQ.
Not this one: Acoustic energy is conserved and converted to heat only through absorption friction or passed/reflected.
Not this one: EQ changes the electrical spectrum fed to loudspeakers; it cannot change the decay time (RT60) of the room.
Not this one: Carpet is a thin porous absorber effective only at high frequencies and provides virtually zero low-frequency transmission loss.

topic: Sabin unit definition and absorption coefficients above 1.0
prompt: In acoustical calculations, what is one 'sabin' of absorption equivalent to, and how can a laboratory-measured absorption coefficient occasionally exceed 1.00?
choices: One sabin equals 100 decibels of transmission loss through lead sheeting

One sabin is the absorption of a unit area (1 m² metric or 1 ft² U.S.) of an open window (100% absorption = 1.00); measured coefficients can slightly exceed 1.00 in random-incidence reverberation chamber tests due to edge diffraction effects
One sabin is the time in seconds for sound to decay by 60 dB
Absorption coefficients range from −100 to +100 ohms
explanation: A sabin represents one unit area (1 m² or 1 ft²) of complete absorption (equivalent to an open window, coefficient 1.00); diffraction around sample edges in reverberation rooms can yield apparent coefficients slightly above 1.0.
studyNote: 1 sabin = 1 unit area (m² or ft²) of open window (α = 1.00). Edge diffraction in lab tests can make α appear > 1.0.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 231-234
rationales: Not this one: Transmission loss is measured in decibels (dB), whereas sabins measure sound absorption.
Correct: One sabin equals the absorption of a unit area of open window (α = 1.00), and edge diffraction can push lab readings above 1.0.
Not this one: The time for a 60 dB decay is Reverberation Time (RT60), measured in seconds.
Not this one: Absorption coefficients are dimensionless ratios between 0 and 1 (plus edge diffraction effects), not ohms.

task: Coordinate with life safety and security professionals
topic: Fatal ground-fault current threshold (120-230 mA across 1 kOhm body resistance)
prompt: Why does a standard 15 A or 20 A thermal-magnetic branch-circuit breaker fail to protect a human being from lethal electrocution during a ground fault, requiring an RCD/GFCI earth-leakage device instead?
choices: A 20 A breaker trips at 0.001 mA, which is too sensitive for human contact
Human body resistance is roughly 1,000,000 ohms, so 240 V produces no current
With human body resistance around 1 kΩ, a ground-fault current of only 120 mA (on 120 V) to 230 mA (on 230 V) can be fatal—far below the 15 A or 20 A overload threshold of a standard circuit breaker
Standard circuit breakers monitor only optical fiber cables
explanation: Overcurrent breakers protect building wiring from overload/short-circuit fires at 15–20 A, whereas a fatal shock through a ~1 kΩ human body requires only ~120 to 230 mA; earth-leakage devices (GFCI/RCD) trip at 10–100 mA within 5–100 ms to save lives.
studyNote: Overload breaker protects wire (15–20 A); RCD/GFCI protects people (trips at 10–100 mA in 5–100 ms; 120–230 mA across ~1 kΩ body is fatal).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 209-212
rationales: Not this one: A 20 A breaker requires >20,000 mA to trip, not 0.001 mA.
Not this one: Effective human body resistance under shock conditions is around 1 kΩ (1,000 Ω), allowing lethal current at mains voltage.
Correct: A ~120–230 mA current through the body (~1 kΩ) is fatal yet far too small to trip a 15–20 A overload breaker.
Not this one: Circuit breakers protect copper AC/DC electrical circuits.

task: Coordinate with life safety and security professionals
topic: Three stakeholder groups in networked AV security (Operational, Network, Physical)
prompt: When coordinating security for a networked AV installation under Chapter 18, which three distinct stakeholder groups must the CTS-D engage?
choices: Marketing, Catering, and Landscaping stakeholders
Audio, Video, and Lighting sales representatives only
Shipping, Receiving, and Billing clerks
Operational stakeholders (data owners who decide what to protect), Network stakeholders (ports, firewalls, routers, access control), and Physical stakeholders (rooms, racks, locks, tamper prevention)
explanation: Comprehensive AV security coordination requires engaging Operational stakeholders (data/content owners), Network stakeholders (IT/firewall/routing administrators), and Physical security stakeholders (facility access, cabinet locks, visual privacy).
studyNote: Three security stakeholder areas: Operational (data owners), Network (IT/firewalls/ports), and Physical (spaces/racks/tamper).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 18, pp. 372-375
rationales: Not this one: These roles do not govern information, network, or facility security.
Not this one: Vendor sales reps do not own the client's operational data, enterprise firewall, or building security.
Not this one: Logistics staff do not set cybersecurity or physical security policy.
Correct: Chapter 18 divides security stakeholders into Operational, Network, and Physical domains.

task: Coordinate with life safety and security professionals
topic: Power strip daisy-chaining rules and bundled power cable heat hazard
prompt: What electrical safety and fire-code precautions does Chapter 10 highlight regarding power strips and tightly bundled AC mains power cables?
choices: Never plug one free-standing power strip into another (daisy-chaining; check AHJ rules for rack PDUs plugged into wall receptacles), and never bundle high-current power cables tightly together without ventilation because trapped heat creates a fire hazard
Daisy-chaining five free-standing power strips in series increases circuit capacity from 15 A to 75 A
Bundling 30 high-current mains cords inside thermal insulation improves power factor
Protective-earth pins should be removed when plugging a rack PDU into a wall outlet
explanation: Daisy-chaining free-standing power strips is a code violation and overload risk, and tightly bundling high-current power cables traps heat, degrades insulation, and creates a fire hazard.
studyNote: Never daisy-chain free-standing power strips, and keep high-current power cables ventilated rather than tightly bundled.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 213-216, 220
rationales: Correct: Free-standing power strips must not be daisy-chained, and power cables require ventilation to prevent dangerous heat buildup.
Not this one: Daisy-chaining strips adds contact resistance and overload risk without increasing branch-circuit breaker capacity.
Not this one: Trapping heat in bundled power cables accelerates insulation breakdown and fire risk.
Not this one: Protective-earth connections must remain unbroken on every PDU and enclosure.

task: Coordinate with site or project specific professionals
topic: De facto standards vs formal ANSI/ISO standards in trade coordination
prompt: When coordinating equipment interfaces with allied professionals, what distinguishes a 'de facto standard' from a formal standard accredited by a body such as ANSI or ISO?
choices: A de facto standard is a mandatory federal law enforced by prison sentences
A de facto standard is widely accepted and used by industry or the public through market adoption, even though it was not necessarily written or approved by an official standards body
A de facto standard prohibits interoperability between products
Formal ANSI standards are secret documents that only one manufacturer may read
explanation: A formal standard is developed by a recognized standards organization (such as ANSI/AVIXA, ISO, or IEEE), whereas a de facto standard achieves widespread adoption through industry practice without necessarily having formal standards-body ratification.
studyNote: Formal standard = ratified by an accredited standards body (ANSI/AVIXA, ISO); De facto standard = widely adopted by market/industry practice.
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 152-155
rationales: Not this one: A mandatory law is a regulation or statute, not a de facto standard.
Correct: De facto standards arise from broad market and industry acceptance rather than formal standards-body accreditation.
Not this one: Both technical and de facto standards facilitate compatibility and consistent practice.
Not this one: Accredited ANSI/AVIXA standards are open, vendor-neutral consensus documents.

task: Coordinate with site or project specific professionals
topic: ANSI/AVIXA 2M-2010 and D401.01 standard guide for design and coordination
prompt: Which AVIXA standard guide defines the four-phase framework (Concept Design, Design, Construction, Verification) and the coordination processes, deliverables, and meetings required across an audiovisual project?
choices: ANSI/AVIXA F501.01:2015
ANSI/AVIXA V201.01:2021
ANSI/AVIXA 2M-2010 / ANSI/AVIXA D401.01 (Standard Guide for Audiovisual Systems Design and Coordination Processes)
ANSI/ASA S12.60
explanation: ANSI/AVIXA 2M-2010 (revised as ANSI/AVIXA D401.01) is the Standard Guide for Audiovisual Systems Design and Coordination Processes, defining project phases, deliverables, meetings, and the ~150-item coordination checklist.
studyNote: D401.01 (updating 2M-2010) = Standard Guide for AV Systems Design and Coordination Processes (4 phases + 150-item checklist).
source: Official CTS-D Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 3, Chapter 7, & Chapter 19, pp. 31-35, 154, 388-392
